summary: Routing systems have been controlled by relatively static policies, but data centers, on-demand WAN services and dynamic policies need more dynamic programming. This informational RFC states the problem the Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) addresses.

eli5.summary: Routers usually follow fixed instructions, but modern networks want to change them quickly with software. This explains why.

questions: why interface to the routing system
why not use snmp to configure routers
what is the interface to the routing system
subtitle: Why routers need a fast, programmable, standard interface that software can use to read and change routing state.

tldr.problem: Routing has been steered by fairly static policy, but data centers, on-demand WAN services and real-time security responses need applications to read and change routing state quickly. Today that is done with proprietary tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC argues for a data-model-driven Interface to the Routing System (I2RS): an I2RS client talks to an I2RS agent on the router using a protocol with features such as fine-grained locking, multiple simultaneous operations and filtered notifications.
tldr.outcome: It only states the problem and lists the properties a protocol needs. It does not define a protocol, and it leaves open whether existing mechanisms are extended or a new one is built.

today: RFC 7920 is an Informational problem statement and no obsoleting or updating RFC is listed for it. The companion architecture is RFC 7921.

sections.title: Why Routing Needs a Programmable Interface
sections.content:
Routing systems have traditionally used routing and signaling (for example MPLS) to control forwarding, with route computation guided by relatively static policies such as link cost, route cost, or import and export policy. The RFC lists new pressures: highly dynamic data-center networking, on-demand WAN services, policy-driven traffic steering and service chaining, real-time security responses through traffic control, and moving policy decisions out of the router itself.

These pressures call for ways to control routing information and traffic paths, and to pull out topology, traffic statistics and other analytics. The RFC says that the scale of modern networks makes automating even simple operations necessary, and that an application needs a feedback loop so it can verify its changes and react to network changes.

Proprietary solutions already cover some cases. The RFC reasons that this makes a common, publicly documented interface feasible, and that standardizing it will make integration easier.
sections.eli5: Networks changed faster than the old way of steering them. Apps now want to give directions and check they worked, and everyone should be able to use the same language to do it.

sections.title: The I2RS Model and Its Scope
sections.content:
The RFC calls for a data-model-driven interface plus at least one protocol with clearly defined operations. Two roles matter. The I2RS agent sits with a routing element, which may or may not be co-located with a data plane. The I2RS client may be built into a network application or used by one or more applications, for instance as part of a network controller or orchestration system that offers a non-I2RS interface to applications.

Only the client, the agent and the protocol between them are inside the scope of I2RS standardization. The policy database, topology database, subscription and configuration templates, routing and signaling protocols, the RIB manager and the FIB manager and data plane are outside it, although the agent interacts with them, both writing (policy databases, RIB manager) and reading (measurements, topology).

Data models should describe the meaning and relationships of items, be separable by feature, versioned and extendable, and translate into a concise transfer syntax that applications find easy to use. Transfer should reuse existing transport protocols for reliability, security and timeliness.
sections.eli5: There is a messenger on the app side (the client) and a listener inside the router (the agent). Only how they talk is being designed; the rest of the router stays as it is.

sections.title: Routing State and Router Information
sections.content:
Section 3 asks I2RS to focus on data models for the RIB layer (the RIB, Label Information Base, multicast RIB and policy-based routing). The desired state can range from static routes to policy-based routing to static multicast replication. To model next hops usefully, the model must handle next-hop indirection and recursion (a prefix X routed like prefix Y) and different kinds of tunneling and encapsulation.

The RFC contrasts this with efforts that standardize forwarding-plane models, such as ForCES (RFC 3746). Using routing indirection, recursion and abstractions like tunnels and LSPs offers more flexibility than collapsing state into individual FIB routes that must each be changed when something moves. Policies and parameters of routing and signaling protocols should also be configurable dynamically.

Section 4 covers reading information. Applications need topology, verification that programmed state is installed, flow measurements and existing configuration. Even BGP-LS (RFC 7752) only shows the current active state, while applications also need potentially available (for example administratively down) or unknown paths and links. Applications should be able to request measurements dynamically, with data possibly delivered through IPFIX (RFC 5470), and to get event notifications such as route installed, route changed or primary LSP changed, which MIB notifications mostly do not provide.
sections.eli5: The app wants to change the router's map in smart ways, like saying "send X the way you send Y", and to ask the router what it sees and be told when something changes.

sections.title: Aspects of an I2RS Protocol
sections.content:
Section 5 lists the key aspects of an interface to the routing system. Whether they are met by extending existing mechanisms or by something new is left for further investigation.

  • Multiple simultaneous asynchronous operations: independent atomic operations without waiting for each to finish.
  • Very fine granularity of data locking for writing: lock something like a particular prefix and route rather than coarse configuration.
  • Multi-headed control: several applications may talk to one agent in a minimally coordinated way; data can be owned by different clients at different times. Details are in RFC 7921.
  • Duplex: either side can initiate communication and send events, acknowledgements or failures at any time. It is not a pure pull model.
  • High throughput: for example 10,000 operations per second.
  • Low latency: simple operations such as reading or writing one prefix route in a sub-second timescale.
  • Multiple channels: data may come from different router components. Writes are only expected on channels with authorization and authentication.
  • Scalable, filterable information access.
  • Secure control and access: authentication and authorization, integrity protection, and in most cases confidentiality.
  • Extensibility and interoperability across versions of protocols and models.
sections.eli5: The list says the messenger system must be quick, let many apps share a router without bumping into each other, work in both directions, and keep strangers out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC treats security as a key aspect because the interface can install state and extract detailed router state. The need for secure control and access is set out in the requirements list, and architectural security considerations are in RFC 7921.

In brief, the I2RS agent is assumed to have a separate authentication and authorization channel to validate a client's identity and permissions. Mutual authentication between agent and client is required, and different levels of integrity, confidentiality and replay protection are relevant for different aspects of I2RS.
sections.eli5: Only trusted apps may give the router directions, and both sides must prove who they are first.

sections.title: Why Not the CLI, SNMP or NETCONF Alone
sections.content:
Appendix A reviews three ways routers are managed. The command-line interface is the most popular and is proprietary. Scraping its human-oriented output is burdensome, and it is unlikely ever to be standardized, so it is not considered a candidate. SNMP with MIB modules is widely used to read state and statistics but very rarely to configure devices, for reasons such as complexity and missing configuration semantics like rollback, so it is not a candidate either.

NETCONF (RFC 6241) overcame many configuration limits, but its adoption has been slow. I2RS will define the information and data models it needs, and multi-headed control may require extensions to NETCONF or to data models.
sections.eli5: The old tools are either too messy, too read-only, or too new for everyone to have adopted. So the RFC asks what a better fit would need.
